text: Over the course of the war, drones went from being scarce and quickly lost to being the main killer on the battlefield.
In 2022 drones were mostly scouts: commercial quadcopters, Ukrainian fixed-wing ISR drones and a few Bayraktar TB2s.
Around 90% of Ukrainian UAVs were lost in 2022.
Only about a third of Ukrainian UAV missions succeeded in 2022.
The Russian Shahed drone campaign against Ukrainian cities began in late September 2022.
In 2023 Russia's 'reconnaissance-fires circuit' of Orlan-10 drones plus artillery, and the Lancet loitering munition, dominated the battlefield.
By autumn 2023 Russian Lancets were hitting Ukrainian jets about 65 km from Russian-held ground.
In 2023 Ukraine was losing about 10,000 UAVs a month to Russian electronic warfare (EW).
The FPV (first-person-view kamikaze quadcopter) boom arrived in 2024.
RUSI's fieldwork found that tactical UAVs caused 60–70% of damaged or destroyed Russian systems in 2024.
RUSI's fieldwork found that 60–80% of FPVs never reached their target in 2024.
Russian Shahed-type launches roughly tripled in 2024 compared with 2023, to about 11,000, most of them after August.
In 2025 a drone 'kill zone' 10–15 km deep formed on both sides of the line.
The Drone Line project, announced in February 2025, was one driver of the 2025 kill zone.
Fibre-optic FPVs with 40+ km reach helped form the 2025 kill zone.
Russia's Rubikon center hunting Ukrainian drone teams and logistics helped form the 2025 kill zone.
Russia launched over 50,000 Shahed-type drones at Ukraine in 2025.
Ukraine was mass-producing interceptor drones at about 950 a day by December 2025.
Russia lost access to Starlink in early February 2026: ISW dates it to 1 February and the Kyiv Independent to 5 February.
The Starlink loss in February 2026 grounded Russia's deeper-reaching strike drones but not its fibre-optic FPVs.
Because Russia's fibre-optic FPVs were unaffected by the Starlink loss, the close kill zone kept growing, to 20–25 km in some sectors by July 2026.
In 2026 Ukrainian ground robots (UGVs) took over a large share of front-line logistics.
In 2026 Russia moved to jet-powered Gerans, which are much harder to intercept.
Ukrainian officials claim drones cause 70–80% of Russian casualties.

text: Four long trends in ISR, C2 and logistics run through all nine eras of the war: growing battlefield transparency, mass becoming a liability, digital cloud-based Ukrainian C2, and logistics becoming the main target.
Battlefield transparency grew over the war and the drone "kill zone" got deeper.
In 2022 surveillance came mainly from Orlan-10 drones, Bayraktar TB2s, commercial and allied satellites and intercepted radio traffic, and artillery did the killing.
In 2022 Russian units with their own drones could put fire on a target 3–5 minutes after spotting it.

In early 2025 RUSI described a dense drone network: the battlefield was fully visible within 3 km of the line of contact, coverage thinned out to about 15 km, and commanders could task reconnaissance out to about 40 km.
In mid-2026 Ukrainian commanders put the zone of regular drone strikes at 20–25+ km on both sides of the line.
One Ukrainian corps commander expects the kill zone to reach 30 km by the end of 2026.
Assault groups shrank over the war: from Russian BTG columns in 2022, to Ukrainian assault detachments of 20 or fewer, to Russian infiltration teams of 1–5 people in 2025–26.
Vehicles now hide in dug-in shelters and dart out to fire, and troops walk the last 10–15+ km to positions.

Ukrainian C2 went digital and cloud-based with Starlink as its backbone: Kropyva, GIS Arta, Delta and its modules (Vezha, Avengers AI, Mission Control, Delta Tube) and the ePoints bonus scheme all ride on Starlink and cellular links.

Russia built a C2 system similar to Ukraine's, with Strelets, drone "reconnaissance-fire circuits" and smuggled Starlink terminals, but Russian C2 has been reported as more centralised and more fragile.

In February 2026 a Starlink speed cap (late January) and then SpaceX's whitelist (enforced 5 February) cut off unregistered Starlink terminals, Russian front-line C2 broke down, and Ukraine made its fastest gains since 2023.
Russia partially recovered its C2 over summer 2026 through mesh radios, other satellites, relays and laundered whitelist registrations; the Ukrainian edge narrowed but did not close.
Logistics became the main target of the war.
In 2022 Ukraine used HIMARS against Russian depots.
In 2024 Ukraine used long-range drones against Russian arsenals such as Toropets and Tikhoretsk.
In 2025 Russian drone units such as Rubikon hunted Ukrainian supply roads.
In 2026 a Ukrainian "middle strike" / "Logistics Lockdown" campaign at 20–200 km depth cut freight on the M-14 by about 71% and caused fuel rationing in Crimea.
Both sides now net their roads, move at night and hand the last mile to ground robots (UGVs, Ukrainian NRK).
Ukraine logged 25,143 UGV missions in August 2026 alone.

In 2022 Russia went into the war with insecure analogue radios, missing encryption keys and stolen civilian phones; its traffic was mostly units reporting their positions, which Ukraine exploited.
In 2023 higher Russian HQs were dispersed and linked by microwave links, relay vehicles and field cable, often tied into captured Ukrainian civilian telecoms.
In 2023 Strelets was used for reconnaissance and fire correction by elite Russian units, while below battalion level traffic stayed mostly in the clear.

By 2025–26 Russia had dropped the goal of one end-to-end automated C2 system (the Sozvezdie-M2 / UTLCS lineage) in favour of task-specific tools: Glaz/Groza for drone-to-fires, ZOV Maps and the Svod situational-awareness complex.
Up to 80% of Russian fire missions are now flown by unmanned systems.

Photos from Russian command posts show ASTRAS, a domestic messenger-style tool (text, voice, probably files) that apparently replaced the blocked Discord; it is a chat system, not a map-centric one like Delta.
Russian C2 is top-down: drones are kept over Russian forces for "combat management", and horizontal coordination between neighbouring units is weak.
In 2024–26 Russian forces depended on smuggled Starlink terminals, bought via Dubai and Central Asia (one analyst claims 50,000+), and on Telegram for coordination and fundraising.
In February 2026 the whitelist removed Starlink from Russian forces, and then the Kremlin throttled Telegram.
Russia's replacements for Starlink and Telegram were Yamal/Express satellite terminals, Gazprom Space Systems ("far less reliable"), mesh networks, radios and cable.

Reported side effects of the Russian communications loss in February 2026 included friendly fire, with 12 killed in one Zaporizhzhia incident, and attempts to get Ukrainians to register terminals for Russian forces.
A Ukrainian USF brigade commander forecast that Russian C2 would take about six months to recover from the Starlink loss.
Biletskyi forecast one or two months for partial recovery of Russian C2 and three to five years for full recovery.
Russian C2 recovery from March to September 2026 was partial, and faster than Ukraine hoped.

Parish and Müller (2001), Procedural Modeling of Cities, grow road networks with an extended L-system under global goals (pattern templates such as a grid, density maps) and local constraints (water, slope), then subdivide blocks into lots.
The kolkhoz landscape suits the Parish–Müller road model with a strong grid goal: straight belt roads at fixed spacing, snapped to the belt grid.
Vanegas et al. (2012), Procedural Generation of Parcels, subdivide blocks by recursive oriented-bounding-box splitting and straight-skeleton subdivision.
Oriented-bounding-box splitting reproduces rectangular field blocks between belts and narrow house plots along a village street.
Emilien et al. (2012), Procedural generation of villages on arbitrary terrains, is a terrain-aware village growth model covering road seeds, parcels and buildings driven by slope and accessibility.
The Emilien et al. village model fits linear villages following valleys and balkas.
Galin et al. (2010), Procedural Generation of Roads, route roads across terrain by weighted shortest path with slope, water and vegetation costs and bridges.
The Galin et al. road model suits inter-village roads crossing gullies and floodplains.
Smelik et al. (2014), A Survey on Procedural Modelling for Virtual Worlds, maps the field across terrain, vegetation, water, roads and settlements.
Patel (2010), Polygon Map Generation, builds maps from Voronoi and Lloyd-relaxed polygons with elevation, moisture and rivers.
Patel's polygon map method suits irregular macro features (woods, catchments, balka networks) but less so the rectilinear field grid.

DeepStateMap is a Ukrainian war map run by the DeepState UA NGO and fed largely by Ukrainian military sources.
DeepStateMap is deliberately published 2–3 days late for operational security.
DeepStateMap's visual grammar is simple: semi-transparent area fills show control status (occupied, liberated, recently liberated, unknown/grey, pre-2022 occupied).
On DeepStateMap, point icons mark Russian units, airfields and HQs, and arrows show "directions of attack".
DeepStateMap never shows Ukrainian positions.
The ISW/CTP map is the Western reference map of the war; its legend is epistemic rather than just territorial, separating assessed (evidence-backed) from claimed (asserted, unverified) areas.
Since December 2025 the ISW/CTP map draws a dedicated infiltration-areas layer.
Most Western outlets, for example the BBC, redraw ISW/CTP data rather than map the front themselves.

From 2025 on, drone kill zones and infiltration by small Russian groups turned the grey zone from a thin no-man's-land into a deep contact zone with overlapping positions: the front line stopped being a line.
The deepening grey zone forced DeepState (2026) and ISW (December 2025) to redefine their map uncertainty categories.
DeepState has clashed publicly with Ukrainian commanders over encirclements and breakthroughs, at Makarivka (December 2024) and Dobropillia (August 2025).
Flag-planting photo-ops by both sides are an information-war tactic that careful mappers refuse to map.
Delta is the Ukrainian Ministry of Defence's situational-awareness system, one of the Ukrainian military's own digital layers.
Kropyva is an Army SOS artillery and mapping tablet app used by the Ukrainian military.
Vezha is a drone-stream module of the Ukrainian military's digital systems, running the Avengers AI.
The Army of Drones Bonus "e-points" system turned video-verified strikes into a points economy with unit leaderboards and a marketplace.
DeepState's undocumented history endpoint serves the full GeoJSON of every DeepStateMap version since 3 April 2022.

Differencing DeepStateMap month-end versions reproduces DeepState's own published monthly territory figures to within a few km² in most months, and gives Russian gains and Ukrainian recaptures separately.
DeepState has no documented API or open licence, although undocumented JSON endpoints exist and community scrapers use them.
ISW's ArcGIS map layers are public but carry "exclusive intellectual property… written consent" terms.
ACLED requires a corporate licence for commercial use of its data.
GeoConfirmed's free API is scoped to "research, journalism, and analytical use".
Liveuamap allows reuse of its maps "with reference" but sells its API.
Among the war-map and symbology resources surveyed, only the symbology renderer milsymbol is permissively (MIT) licensed.
Data rights, not data availability, are the main blocker for using war-map data in the game.

anchor.section: 2. DeepStateMap in depth / 2.1 Who runs it, history

text: According to the live page source, DeepStateMap is built with Leaflet plus a PixiJS WebGL overlay, Highcharts for statistics charts, fabric.js for the drawing tools, and leaflet.pattern for patterned fills.

anchor.section: 2. DeepStateMap in depth / 2.2 Methodology and sourcing

text: DeepState's anti-emotional rule: photos of Russian flags do not move the line. Pohorilyi: "We cannot react emotionally or quickly, or when we see Russians with flags there, we draw…"
DeepState's history endpoint listed 1,771 published DeepStateMap versions between 3 April 2022 and 27 September 2026.
DeepState's /api/history/{id}/geojson endpoint returns the complete map for any listed DeepStateMap version.
The median gap between DeepStateMap versions is about 24 hours.
DeepState published 420 map versions in 2022, then about 360 a year, and 27–31 a month in 2026.

Each DeepStateMap version carries a short changelog in Ukrainian and (from May 2022) English, with links to the affected settlements, e.g. "The Ukrainian Armed Forces liberated Ridkodub, Nove and Katerynivka…" (27 September 2026).
The live DeepStateMap is best understood as one curated daily snapshot plus a news-style change log, not a real-time feed.

anchor.section: 2. DeepStateMap in depth / 2.5 The grey zone and uncertainty

text: On DeepStateMap, grey originally meant "territory where the situation requires clarification", in practice the thin no-man's-land between the two sides' first lines.

anchor.section: 2. DeepStateMap in depth / 2.5 The grey zone and uncertainty

text: In 2025 Ukraine had too few troops to man positions densely, and Russia attacked with small infiltration squads instead of mechanised assaults.

anchor.section: 2. DeepStateMap in depth / 2.5 The grey zone and uncertainty

text: The 2025 shift to infiltration produced "increasingly jagged and unusual formations" on DeepStateMap, with grey now depicting a wide contact zone of overlapping positions.

anchor.section: 2. DeepStateMap in depth / 2.5 The grey zone and uncertainty

text: In 2026 DeepState explained that grey on its map now represents areas where Russian forces have infiltrated.

anchor.section: 2. DeepStateMap in depth / 2.5 The grey zone and uncertainty

text: DeepState says that in its grey areas positions "may effectively overlap or intermix," and grey should not be read as no-man's-land, as either side's control, or as a precise front.

anchor.section: 2. DeepStateMap in depth / 2.5 The grey zone and uncertainty

anchor.section: 2. DeepStateMap in depth / 2.7 Territory time series (km²)

text: The territory series was computed (queried 2026-09-28) from the last published DeepStateMap version of each month, listed by /api/history/public and downloaded via /api/history/{id}/geojson: 55 versions from 3 April 2022 to 27 September 2026.

anchor.section: 2. DeepStateMap in depth / 2.7 Territory time series (km²)

text: In the computed series, Russian-held area is all DeepStateMap polygons filled #a52714 ("Occupied") minus a fixed pre-2022 mask of ORDLO plus Crimea and Tuzla, 43,572 km², taken from the latest version.

anchor.section: 2. DeepStateMap in depth / 2.7 Territory time series (km²)

text: In the computed series, all areas are clipped to Ukraine's land (the geoBoundaries border intersected with Natural Earth 10 m land) and measured in a Lambert azimuthal equal-area projection centred on Ukraine.

anchor.section: 2. DeepStateMap in depth / 2.7 Territory time series (km²)

text: In the computed series, Russian gain is area newly red since the previous month-end, Ukrainian recapture is area red at the previous month-end but not now, and net is the change in total red area.

text: In November 2025 Polymarket overlaid DeepStateMap without permission; DeepState complained and the overlay was removed.
DeepStateMap is operated by the DeepState UA NGO (Ukraine) and styled with semi-transparent control polygons, custom point icons and attack arrows, as a Leaflet web map plus apps.
DeepStateMap's legend categories are occupied, liberated, recently liberated, unknown status (grey/infiltration), pre-2022 occupied and foreign occupied, plus Russian units, airfields and HQs.
DeepStateMap publishes about daily versions, deliberately 2–3 days behind events.
DeepStateMap's data is accessible only through undocumented JSON endpoints; no open licence was found, and DeepState complains about unauthorised commercial reuse.

The ISW/CTP map is operated by the Institute for the Study of War and the AEI Critical Threats Project (USA), as static daily PNG maps in the Russian Offensive Campaign Assessment (ROCA) plus an ArcGIS StoryMap/web map.

The ISW/CTP map's legend categories are assessed Russian-controlled terrain, assessed Russian advances, assessed Russian infiltration areas, claimed Russian territory, claimed Ukrainian counteroffensives, pre-24 February 2022 occupied, control of terrain in Russia and Russian field fortifications, with separate partisan layers.
The ISW/CTP map is updated daily (features stamped pub_date 2026-09-27), with a monthly time-lapse archive.
The ISW/CTP map layers are public ArcGIS Feature Services, but are marked as the "exclusive intellectual property of ISW" requiring "written consent".
The Black Bird Group map is run by a Finnish NGO and draws two-sided front lines plus movement arrows over an OpenFreeMap/OSM basemap in NATO red/blue.
The Black Bird Group map's legend categories are Russian-held territory, front line (Russian side), front line (Ukrainian side), Russian movements and Ukrainian movements.
The Black Bird Group map is "updated regularly" (near daily), and its weekly Friday snapshot feeds ACLED.
Black Bird Group presents its map as a "public product" and welcomes non-profit or public-facing adaptations, but gives no formal licence text.
UA Control Map is run by a pseudonymous operator (unverified) and shows geolocations, front lines and unit positions, with clickable per-feature source links.
UA Control Map is a web "data viewer"; its legend, update cadence and terms of use were not verified.
Liveuamap was founded by two Dnipro software engineers in February 2014 and is now Liveuamap LLC (Virginia, USA) with EU-hosted infrastructure.
Liveuamap is an event-pin map fed by AI web crawlers, fact-checked by analysts and curated by editors, with an archive by day.
Liveuamap's legend is a pictogram per event type (shahed, bomb, drone, explosion, air defence, casualties, speech…) in a side colour.
Liveuamap updates continuously.
Liveuamap allows reuse of its "data and maps… with reference to liveuamap.com", and sells a paid API from $150/month.
GeoConfirmed is run by an international volunteer OSINT collective; every marker is one geolocated clip with sources and a public geolocation breakdown, with timeline playback and ORBAT trees.
GeoConfirmed's legend has 116 icons, each an object type × state (active / recently destroyed / older destroyed), coloured by faction and filterable by date, equipment, unit and faction.

confidence_note: Fetch date not stated exactly; research date 2026-09-28.
text: GeoConfirmed updates continuously, with 883 new Ukraine events in the 30 days before the research fetch (about late September 2026).
GeoConfirmed offers an unauthenticated read API with KMZ/CSV/GeoJSON export, "freely available for research, journalism, and analytical use", with no licence text.
The ACLED Ukraine Conflict Monitor, run by the international NGO ACLED, uses scaled event circles plus an oblast choropleth, with the front line taken from Black Bird Group.
The ACLED Ukraine Conflict Monitor's legend covers political-violence event types, infrastructure tags (energy, health, education, residential) and conservative civilian fatality counts.
The ACLED Ukraine Conflict Monitor publishes weekly situation updates.
ACLED data requires registration; its EULA is non-commercial by default, requires a corporate licence for businesses, bars raw redistribution and makes attribution mandatory.
BBC "Ukraine in maps", by BBC Visual Journalism (UK), is a set of explainer maps with narrative text that redraw ISW/CTP daily assessments of Russian control.
BBC "Ukraine in maps" is updated periodically: first published 24 February 2022, last updated September 2026; it is © BBC.
The New York Times' "Maps: Tracking the Russian Invasion of Ukraine" is a long-running interactive updated periodically through the war; it is © NYT.
The legend of the NYT invasion map was not verified because the fetch was blocked.
Suriyak Maps is an anonymous X/Telegram account (since March 2017), apparently Spanish-speaking, that also maps Syria, Yemen, Libya, the Sahel and Gaza.
Suriyak Maps posts static map images to X (110k followers) and Telegram (47k), frequently, with no stated licence.
Per Wikipedia editors, Suriyak Maps shows control plus war-zone / grey / unknown bands; the legend was not verified.
Andrew Perpetua's "UA map" (ukrdailyupdate.com), made with @Gaspo_sk, is a Leaflet web map built on geolocated footage, with a daily date slider, measuring tools and clustered event badges.
Andrew Perpetua's map uses event badges by type (drone, Shahed, Lancet, helicopter, TOS, flag, death, explosion, abandoned…) in dark blue, dark red, gold and purple.
Andrew Perpetua's map is updated daily (latest map date 26 September 2026); it has no licence and asks for screenshots rather than embedding.
AMK Mapping is a pseudonymous analyst (X, and Telegram with 60k subscribers) covering Ukraine and the Middle East.
AMK Mapping's control map is a Google My Maps map with toggleable layers and publicly exportable KML; it has no licence beyond Google My Maps terms.

AMK Mapping's legend shows confirmed Russian control (brick red), confirmed Ukrainian control (indigo), infiltration zone (black), confirmed Russian advances (yellow), confirmed Ukrainian advances (light blue), direction definitions, points of interest and "Never forget".
AMK Mapping's control map is updated near daily (last update 28 September 2026).
ISW's two epistemic tiers ("assessed" = evidence-backed, "claimed" = asserted but unverified) are the clearest model of confidence as a map layer.
In ISW's web-map JSON, Russian-controlled terrain and Russian advances share a translucent red fill (RGBA 239,0,0,71) with a red outline.
In ISW's web map, infiltration areas are a patterned picture-fill with a dashed red outline.
In ISW's web map, claimed Russian territory is translucent orange (RGBA 255,170,0,126).
In ISW's web map, claimed Ukrainian counteroffensives are translucent light blue (RGBA 115,223,255,147) with a blue outline.
ISW's infiltration feature service was created on 20 December 2025.
Each daily ISW/CTP ROCA pairs a theatre map with per-sector zoom maps, and its text runs axis by axis, each with a stated "Russian objective" and the "assessed objective" of named Russian armies.

ISW backs control changes with "geolocated footage published on" a given date, and every ROCA ends with the note that ISW "uses only publicly available information" and receives no classified material.

confidence_note: Seen only in pass-1 search excerpts; the cited 26 Sep 2026 ROCA does not repeat the sentence (see open questions).
text: Earlier ISW ROCAs state that the map shows "the furthest assessed extent of Russian advances" until open-source evidence shows otherwise, that this may underestimate Ukrainian advances, and that a porous front complicates control of terrain.

ISW keeps two partisan products: "reported but not confirmed Ukrainian partisan warfare" (feature service, 2022–) and a curated "Verified Ukrainian Partisan Attacks" StoryMap that includes only high-confidence events.
Wikipedia editors ruled Suriyak Maps unreliable in 2021 for its anonymity and unclear method.
In 2024 Wikipedia editors split on Suriyak Maps between "partisan" and "very neutral… among the more conservative sources".
One Wikipedia editor's 2024 ranking of war maps put ISW first, DeepState and Andrew Perpetua tied second, and Suriyak, MilitaryLand, Rybar and Liveuamap lower.
The same Wikipedia editor described Andrew Perpetua's map as "mostly based on geolocated footage… a bit cautious in reporting Russian gains".

Andrew Perpetua's map page carries a fundraiser for Ukraine's Khartiia corps.

AMK Mapping's legend is a close relative of DeepState's: it uses the same Google-palette reds and blues (#A52714 for Russian control, #0288D1 for Ukrainian advances) and adds explicit advance layers and a black infiltration zone.
AMK Mapping's advance layers are the "change this period" layer that DeepStateMap only implies with its two-week blue "recently liberated" state.
Liveuamap does not document its legend; in a captured feed each event carries a pictogram-colour code, with Russian strikes coded shahed-1, bomb-1 and destroy-1.

In a captured Liveuamap feed, Ukrainian drone strikes on Russia, explosions in Kursk, Ukrainian air defence, casualties in Ukraine and Zelensky statements are coded drone-2, explode-2, aa-2, medicine-2 and speech-2, and a US Congress item speech-10.
Liveuamap's page loads red, blue, green, white and black icon sets; the reading "1 = red = Russian, 2 = blue = Ukrainian" is an inference from 19 captured events.
GeoConfirmed's icon grammar is the most game-ready of the war maps: every object type has three states, active, "recently destroyed/damaged [visible in footage]" and "older destroyed".
On GeoConfirmed, colour is the faction doing the act ("colour of who is shelling"); a killed civilian is drawn "in the colour of who is assessed as doing the attack", and brown means UXO.
GeoConfirmed's object types range from tanks, APCs and trucks to suicide and multipurpose UGVs, short- and long-range one-way attack drones, interceptions, trenches, mines and CBRN incidents.
GeoConfirmed's faction colours for Ukraine are: Ukraine #0051CA, Ukraine civilian #3184FF, Russia #E00000, Russia civilian #FF6666, North Korea #6A1D00, Belarus #400080.
Black Bird Group says of its control areas: "When we paint an area as Russian or Ukrainian-controlled, it's more like here the Ukrainians or Russians generally have more control than the other side."
Black Bird Group values being able to say its map is based on open sources.
NATO APP-6 (STANAG 2019) and US MIL-STD-2525 are aligned military symbology standards; APP-6A (1999) is equivalent to MIL-STD-2525A.
Later APP-6 editions are APP-6B (2008) and APP-6C (2011), and APP-6E is listed as current.
milsymbol supports MIL-STD-2525C/D/E, FM 1-02.2 and APP-6 B/D/E.
In APP-6 and MIL-STD-2525, affiliation is encoded twice, by frame shape and by colour.
In APP-6/MIL-STD-2525 symbology, a friend unit is drawn with a rectangle frame in blue.
In APP-6/MIL-STD-2525 symbology, a hostile unit is drawn with a diamond frame in red.
In APP-6/MIL-STD-2525 symbology, a neutral unit is drawn with a square frame in green.
In APP-6/MIL-STD-2525 symbology, a unknown unit is drawn with a quatrefoil frame in yellow.
APP-6/MIL-STD-2525 have further affiliation states: pending, assumed friend, suspect, and exercise variants.
Because the frame shape carries affiliation as well as colour, APP-6/MIL-STD-2525 symbols work in monochrome.
In APP-6/MIL-STD-2525, a solid frame means present and a dashed frame means planned/anticipated.
In APP-6/MIL-STD-2525, closed frames denote land and sea surface, bottom-open frames air/space, and top-open frames subsurface.

An APP-6/MIL-STD-2525 symbol consists of a frame, a central icon and an optional fill, with modifiers/amplifiers arranged around the frame: unique designation, additional information, altitude/depth, combat effectiveness, headquarters/task force/dummy, and echelon/mobility.

Echelons are coded in the SIDC and drawn above the frame: Team/Crew, Squad, Section, Platoon/detachment, Company/battery/troop, Battalion/squadron, Regiment/group, Brigade, Division, Corps, Army, Army Group/front, Region/Theatre, Command.
Older symbology standards use letter-based symbol identification codes (SIDCs), 15 characters long in the APP-6A lineage.
Current MIL-STD-2525D/E and APP-6D/E use numeric SIDCs; milsymbol's README example is a 30-digit SIDC, and milsymbol implements both the letter and numeric schemes.
milsymbol, by Måns Beckman (spatialillusions), is a pure-JavaScript military symbol renderer under the MIT licence with SVG or Canvas output.
milsymbol renders filled/unfilled and framed/unframed symbols, text fields and movement indicators.
Since v3.0 milsymbol renders every SIDC version with MIL-STD-2525E/APP-6E appearance; its latest release is v3.0.4 (March 2026).
milsymbol has integrations for Leaflet, OpenLayers and Cesium.
milsymbol is the safe choice for game assets, for example by pre-rendering SVGs to a texture atlas at build time.
Spatial Illusions' "Battle Staff Tools" (the "unit generator") is a browser tool for MIL-STD-2525E/APP-6E and 2525C/APP-6B symbols with PNG/SVG export, ORBAT building and a map.
Battle Staff Tools is © 2025 Måns Beckman; it is free on spatialillusions.com with watermarks and donation prompts, but offline use or use on other sites needs a paid licence file.
Battle Staff Tools exports should be treated as not cleared for redistribution in a game.
Black Bird Group explicitly uses the NATO convention "red is the Russian adversary, blue is Ukrainian".
Delta was "built according to NATO standards".
DeepStateMap does not use APP-6 frames.

Delta (Дельта) is a situational-awareness and battlefield-management system developed by the Ukrainian Ministry of Defence's Centre for Innovation and Development of Defence Technologies with the Aerorozvidka NGO.

Delta fuses reports from reconnaissance units, drones, sensors, satellite imagery, partner intelligence and vetted civilians, and maps geolocated data in real time "along with pictures of enemy assets".
Delta is cloud-native and runs on PCs, laptops, tablets and phones.
Delta was first tested in 2017 in a NATO context.
Delta became broadly operational in August 2022.
Delta was publicly unveiled at the NATO TIDE Sprint in Virginia Beach in October 2022.

No documented public DeepState API or open licence was found; the DeepStateMap web app itself calls JSON endpoints.
DeepState's …/api/history/public endpoint lists every map version with Ukrainian/English changelog text and timestamps.
DeepState's …/api/history/{id}/geojson endpoint serves the full map of any listed version, the basis of the computed territory series.
DeepState's …/api/history/last endpoint serves a GeoJSON FeatureCollection with KML-style fill/stroke/styleUrl properties and trilingual names (Ukrainian /// English /// i18n key).

The community scraper cyterat/deepstate-map-data (GPL-3.0 code) provides daily GeoJSON since 2024-07-08, merging "Occupied", "CADR and CALR" and "Occupied Crimea" into one occupied multipolygon, plus a consolidated gzip history.

confidence_note: The file says these are not individually cited.
text: Other DeepState scrapers found on GitHub include a KML exporter and a GIF generator.
The scraper's GPL licence covers its code, not DeepState's data.
DeepState has objected to unauthorised commercial overlays of its map, such as Polymarket's.
For a commercial game, DeepState should be asked for permission, or its map used only as an internal reference.

ISW/CTP layers are public ArcGIS Feature Services queryable via REST, e.g. VIEW_RussiaCoTinUkraine_V2, View_AssessedRussianInfiltrationAreasinUkraine_V4, VIEW_ClaimedUkrainianCounteroffensives_V2 and RUAF_Field_Fortifications_Polylines.
Every ISW ArcGIS item states: "This geodata is the exclusive intellectual property of the Institute for the Study of War (ISW). You may not use this geodata without the written consent of ISW."
ACLED covers non-commercial use with a royalty-free, non-exclusive licence; commercial businesses need a corporate licence and governments a public-sector licence.
Under ACLED's EULA no direct access to raw data may be given, derivatives must be "transformative", and attribution is mandatory.
The ACLED Ukraine Conflict Monitor needs a login for curated files.

GeoConfirmed's API spec states that read endpoints need no authentication and that the data is "freely available for research, journalism, and analytical use", with per-conflict KMZ, CSV and GeoJSON exports.
GeoConfirmed's API spec has no licence field and does not mention commercial use; it asks for a descriptive User-Agent and fair use, and to "get in touch" for bulk or near-real-time needs.
For a commercial game GeoConfirmed should be asked for permission, but its icon grammar (type × state × actor colour) is an idea that can be reimplemented freely.
Liveuamap's terms (January 2023 snapshot) allow use of "our data and maps, including map tiles and areas polygons partially, or in the whole in your work, with reference to liveuamap.com".
Under Liveuamap's terms, third-party images and text stay under their platforms' terms.
Liveuamap's API is paid: Pro costs $150/month for 200 requests/day, and Enterprise starts at $1,000/month.
AMK Mapping's Google My Map exports as KML.
Andrew Perpetua's map asks for screenshots rather than embeds.
Neither AMK Mapping nor Andrew Perpetua states a licence, so both maps should be treated as reference only.
Suriyak publishes its maps as images.
Black Bird Group presents its map as a public product and welcomes non-profit or public-facing adaptations, but has no formal licence, so permission should be asked.
milsymbol is MIT-licensed and fine to ship in the game.
Spatial Illusions' Battle Staff Tools is proprietary.

The research recommends shipping the game with self-authored, simplified historical control polygons (e.g. digitised by hand at era granularity), crediting DeepState, ISW and Black Bird Group as inspiration, and requesting explicit permission before bundling any of their geometry.

Modern RTS and tactical games such as Broken Arrow, WARNO, Regiments and Combat Mission: Black Sea model massed combined arms between NATO-style and Russian forces.
